performed_via_github_app.description:
Codecov provides highly integrated tools to group, merge, archive and compare coverage reports. Whether your team is comparing changes in a pull request or reviewing a single commit, Codecov will improve the code review workflow and quality.

## Code coverage done right.®

1. Upload coverage reports from your CI builds.
2. Codecov merges all builds and languages into one beautiful coherent report.
3. Get commit statuses, pull request comments and coverage overlay via our browser extension.

When Codecov merges your uploads it keeps track of the CI provider (inc. build details) and user specified context, e.g. `#unittest` ~ `#smoketest` or `#oldcode` ~ `#newcode`. You can track the `#unittest` coverage independently of other groups. [Learn more here](
http://docs.codecov.io/docs/flags)

Through **Codecov's Browser Extension** reports overlay directly in GitHub UI to assist in code review in [Chrome](https://chrome.google.com/webstore/detail/codecov/gedikamndpbemklijjkncpnolildpbgo) or Firefox (https://addons.mozilla.org/en-US/firefox/addon/codecov/)

*Highly detailed* **pull request comments** and *customizable* **commit statuses** will improve your team's workflow and code coverage incrementally.

**File backed configuration** all through the `codecov.yml`. 

## FAQ
- Do you **merge multiple uploads** to the same commit? **Yes**
- Do you **support multiple languages** in the same project? **Yes**
- Can you **group coverage reports** by project and/or test type? **Yes**
- How does **pricing** work? Only paid users can view reports and post statuses/comments.

body: Default the debug sidebar to everything collapsed. Otherwise there's too much navigation.

🤖 > Default the debug sidebar to everything collapsed. Otherwise there's too much navigation.

Done. Rather than adding every title to the collapsed list, the sidebar settings now store the inverse — `debug_expanded` instead of `debug_collapsed` — so nothing is open until you open it: every section *and* every field, including `InfoExp`, `ctx`, `co_ctx`, `user_term` and `Segment`.

Inverting it also retired the hardcoded list of section titles in `Settings.re` that had to match `<X>Section.title` by hand, and it covers the per-field labels that list couldn't have reached anyway. Existing persisted settings still load rather than resetting — the sidebar settings record allows extra fields, so a stored `debug_collapsed` from an earlier build is ignored (persistence goes through sexp only, see `Store.F`).

The gating predicate reads positively now:

```reason
let panel_open = title =>
  settings.show_debug_panel && SidebarModel.Settings.is_debug_expanded(title, sidebar);
```

Replies to the individual review threads are inline; the two commits are 7ea565be6a (review pass) and cf90451076 (a follow-up moving the last pre-digested arguments into the collectors).
Look into david's performance profiling stuff.

🤖 > Look into david's performance profiling stuff.

There's prior art worth linking to. David's #2161 (`perf-bench`) is an offline harness measuring the syntax and statics pipeline across cached and uncached scenarios, comparing results across commits. Andrew's `hazel bench-eval`, which landed with #2404, times evaluation on its own. Both are profiling: a controlled run over a fixed program, producing a number you compare against another commit's.

This PR is telemetry rather than profiling. It instruments the shipped app and reports the work an actual editing session is doing — real programs, real keystrokes, including the worker round trip that neither of the others touches. That's a different axis from theirs, not a competing answer on the same one, which is also why it lives behind the debug sidebar and collects nothing while the panels are closed.

Two places the two do overlap, worth converging on before both land:

**The timing primitive, and the shape it records into.** `PhaseTiming.record(label, f)` on `perf-bench` and `TimeUtil.timed(f)` here both wrap a thunk and take wall-clock behind an enable flag, but they record differently. `PhaseTiming` appends to a flat global list of `(label, duration)` pairs that a harness drains after a run. `PerfMetrics` accumulates into a typed `frame` record, commits it once per update cycle, and keeps a bounded newest-first history for the panels. A label stream suits a harness; a per-frame schema suits a live table.

**Granularity.** His instrumentation names sub-phases inside the pipeline — the individual steps within statics and within syntax. This PR times statics and syntax as single units.

What I'd want out of that eventually: one set of instrumentation points, declared in a typed and structured way rather than each site side-effecting a global ref, with two consumers behind it — telemetry into the bounded per-frame history the production app shows, profiling into the labeled accumulator an offline script drains. Both approaches deserve to exist and neither should have to own the call sites. Between the two, `TimeUtil` is the better base to build that on: it returns a typed `Core.Time_ns.Span.t`, and it doesn't reach through `Js_of_ocaml.Js.Unsafe` from `src/util`, which matters for the de-webbing work.

Nothing needs to change in this PR for that. But it's worth settling before we end up with two sets of timing calls threaded through the same pipeline.
